roadmaps.title: AI + Data Engineering
roadmaps.requires: Advanced: finish the AI Engineering or the Data Engineering roadmap first.

domains.title: Python
domains.description: Write understandable, testable programs before adding models.

modules.title: Mutability, copying, scope and function contracts

guide.goal: Write reliable Python programs before connecting AI tools.
guide.checkpoint: Build a JSON-based study tracker with functions, validation, logging and tests.
guide.bridge: You can now organise your code, collaborate in Git and understand HTTP requests.

domains.title: Engineering foundations
domains.description: Use the tools and contracts that make a team project maintainable.

guide.goal: Turn scripts into a maintainable, tested team repository.
guide.checkpoint: Open a pull request with a tested HTTP/JSON utility and reproducible setup instructions.
guide.bridge: Use these engineering habits while learning how data and mathematical operations work.

domains.title: Mathematics and data
domains.description: Understand the operations and data quality behind model behavior.

modules.title: Partial derivatives, Jacobians and vector gradients
Confidence intervals, bootstrap and causal limits

guide.goal: Understand the data, shapes, gradients and statistics behind AI.
guide.checkpoint: Clean a small dataset, plot its distributions and explain a dot product and gradient calculation.
guide.bridge: You are ready to serve validated data and predictions through an API.

domains.title: Machine learning
domains.description: Train reliable baselines and understand what their evaluation actually measures.

modules.title: Decision trees, bagging and boosting mechanisms

guide.goal: Train and evaluate classical models without leakage.
guide.checkpoint: Compare a baseline and two models on a held-out test set; explain metrics and error cases.
guide.bridge: Use the same evaluation discipline when moving from classical models to neural networks.

domains.title: Deep learning
domains.description: Understand training mechanics, architectures and practical optimization.

modules.title: Distributed training: ranks, synchronization and effective batches
Profiling, memory bandwidth and kernel optimization decisions

guide.goal: Understand neural networks, backpropagation and practical optimisation.
guide.checkpoint: Train a small CPU PyTorch model; compare optimisers, save a checkpoint and explain tensor shapes.
guide.bridge: Attention and transformers prepare you to understand and use pretrained language models.

domains.title: LLM engineering
domains.description: Build grounded, bounded language-model features with a free local path.

modules.title: Model cards, licences and reproducible model selection
Structured output, streaming and cancellation contracts
Preference data, DPO and post-training evaluation

guide.goal: Choose and use language models with deliberate prompts, context and outputs.
guide.checkpoint: Build a structured-output assistant with schema validation, recorded-response tests and a local-model option.
guide.bridge: Ground its answers in your own documents through retrieval and citations.

domains.title: Backend and databases
domains.description: Expose reliable APIs and protect shared application state.

guide.goal: Build the API and database layer that an AI application needs.
guide.checkpoint: Build a FastAPI service with validated inputs, a SQL query and API tests.
guide.bridge: Next, learn what a predictive model does so you can compare and serve its results.

domains.title: Retrieval and RAG
domains.description: Connect answers to maintained evidence and evaluate retrieval independently.

modules.title: Document parsing, OCR limits and source provenance
Approximate nearest neighbors and index tradeoffs

guide.goal: Retrieve useful evidence and connect answers to traceable sources.
guide.checkpoint: Build a document search pipeline with chunking, hybrid retrieval, citations and retrieval measurements.
guide.bridge: Measure the complete system and test hostile inputs before giving it more autonomy.

domains.title: Evaluation and security
domains.description: Make quality, safety and failure behavior measurable.

modules.title: Output handling, model supply chains and resource limits

guide.goal: Measure quality and protect the application against predictable failures.
guide.checkpoint: Create a golden dataset, regression report and prompt-injection tests with explicit failure handling.
guide.bridge: Use these checks and permission boundaries when adding tools, workflows and agents.

domains.title: Agents and MCP
domains.description: Build bounded tool workflows before increasing autonomy.

modules.title: MCP versions, discovery and authorization boundaries

guide.goal: Build bounded tool workflows with state, recovery and human approval.
guide.checkpoint: Implement a tool workflow with an MCP connection, approval for sensitive actions and recovery tests.
guide.bridge: Deploy the tested workflow with containers, monitoring and reliable operations.

domains.title: Coding agents
domains.description: Direct and verify generated work with clear engineering context.

guide.goal: Direct coding agents using clear specifications and verify their work.
guide.checkpoint: Write AGENTS.md and a task specification; review a generated change using tests and security checks.
guide.bridge: Connect these engineering capabilities to user needs, product decisions and documentation.

domains.title: Deployment and operations
domains.description: Release reproducible services and observe their real behavior.

modules.title: Backup, restore and data recovery drills

guide.goal: Package and operate an AI service reliably within a small budget.
guide.checkpoint: Run the API in Docker Compose with health checks, timeouts, logs and a documented rollback.
guide.bridge: Use coding agents to maintain the service while keeping review and verification under your control.

domains.title: Product and documentation
domains.description: Build useful products and document only what guides real decisions.

guide.goal: Deliver a useful AI product with evidence, feedback and maintainable documentation.
guide.checkpoint: Ship a small capstone with requirements, architecture, evaluation, deployment instructions and a runbook.
guide.bridge: Choose a team capstone, gather user feedback and revisit the lessons revealed by real failures.

domains.title: Data Engineering
domains.description: A 7-phase data engineering roadmap: distributed processing, orchestration, streaming and CDC, lakehouse storage, modeling, data quality and cloud infrastructure. It builds on the shared Python, engineering, mathematics/data and backend foundation.

guide.goal: Extend the shared Python, SQL and backend foundation into production data pipelines: Spark, Airflow, Kafka/CDC, lakehouse tables, dbt models, quality checks and cloud infrastructure.
guide.checkpoint: Build and explain a reproducible CDC-to-lakehouse pipeline with quality gates, lineage and a recovery test.
guide.bridge: Continue with the advanced AI + Data Engineering roadmap to put models and LLMs on top of this platform.

domains.title: AI + Data Engineering
domains.description: An advanced roadmap for learners who finished the AI Engineering or the Data Engineering roadmap: ML engineering and MLOps on data platforms, LLM and GenAI engineering over data, and system design with interview preparation. It does not repeat either roadmap; review the linked lessons of the roadmap you did not take when a topic is new to you.

guide.goal: Combine a data platform with ML and LLM systems: MLOps on lakehouse data, GenAI over governed data, and end-to-end system design.
guide.checkpoint: Serve a measured ML or RAG consumer from a gold-layer table and defend its system design, failure recovery and trade-offs.
guide.bridge: Start after finishing the AI Engineering or the Data Engineering roadmap. When a topic comes from the roadmap you did not take, open its linked lesson instead of expecting it to be repeated here.

lessons.title: Mutability, copying, scope and function contracts
lessons.why: Mutability, copying, scope and function contracts helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Mutability, copying, scope and function contracts

concepts.name: Object identity
concepts.explanation: Two names may reference one mutable object; assignment does not copy its contents.
concepts.example: Assign b=a for a list, append through b and compare a with a copied list.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming assignment produces an independent list.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which names see the appended element?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Assign b=a for a list, append through b and compare a with a copied list.

concepts.name: Shallow versus deep copy
concepts.explanation: A shallow copy creates an outer container but preserves references to nested objects.
concepts.example: Copy a list of dictionaries and change a nested tag list.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming list.copy also copies nested dictionaries.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which copy operation isolates nested edits?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Copy a list of dictionaries and change a nested tag list.

concepts.name: Mutable defaults
concepts.explanation: Default argument objects are created at function definition time and may survive multiple calls.
concepts.example: Compare a default list parameter with a None sentinel that constructs a fresh list.
concepts.commonMistake: Reusing a default list as if it were new per call.
concepts.checkQuestion: Why does the second call contain the first call's result?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare a default list parameter with a None sentinel that constructs a fresh list.

concepts.name: Local scope and closures
concepts.explanation: Name lookup follows lexical scope; rebinding differs from mutating an existing object.
concepts.example: Return two counter closures and inspect whether their captured state is independent.
concepts.commonMistake: Confusing local rebinding with changing an outer variable.
concepts.checkQuestion: Where is the counter state stored?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Return two counter closures and inspect whether their captured state is independent.

concepts.name: Pure function contracts
concepts.explanation: A pure transformation returns results without changing its inputs, simplifying testing and reuse.
concepts.example: Normalize a record while asserting the original dictionary is unchanged.
concepts.commonMistake: Mutating a caller's object without documenting the side effect.
concepts.checkQuestion: What invariant should hold for the input after a call?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Normalize a record while asserting the original dictionary is unchanged.

concepts.name: Conditional probability
concepts.explanation: P(A given B) restricts the denominator to cases where B occurred.
concepts.example: Use 1000 fictional cases with 10 positives and calculate precision from the confusion table.
concepts.commonMistake: Swapping P(test positive given disease) with P(disease given test positive).
concepts.checkQuestion: Which denominator changes when conditioning?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Use 1000 fictional cases with 10 positives and calculate precision from the confusion table.

concepts.name: Bayes rule
concepts.explanation: A posterior combines the prior with a likelihood and normalizes over competing explanations.
concepts.example: Compare a detector at 1 percent and 20 percent prevalence with unchanged sensitivity.
concepts.commonMistake: Ignoring the base rate when interpreting a positive result.
concepts.checkQuestion: Why can most positive results be false at low prevalence?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare a detector at 1 percent and 20 percent prevalence with unchanged sensitivity.

concepts.name: Likelihood versus probability
concepts.explanation: Likelihood evaluates parameter choices against fixed observed data; it is not a probability distribution over parameters by itself.
concepts.example: Compare the likelihood of eight heads in ten tosses under p=.5 and p=.8.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating a likelihood value as a normalized posterior.
concepts.checkQuestion: What extra information creates a posterior?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare the likelihood of eight heads in ten tosses under p=.5 and p=.8.

concepts.name: Expectation and variance
concepts.explanation: Expectation averages outcomes weighted by probability; variance measures spread around that mean.
concepts.example: Compute the mean and variance of a three-outcome discrete variable.
concepts.commonMistake: Using an unweighted mean for outcomes with unequal probabilities.
concepts.checkQuestion: How does changing a rare large outcome affect variance?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compute the mean and variance of a three-outcome discrete variable.

concepts.name: Decision costs
concepts.explanation: A decision threshold depends on false-positive and false-negative consequences, not just the largest predicted probability.
concepts.example: Compare expected costs of reviewing or accepting a fictional alert.
concepts.commonMistake: Choosing a threshold without stating the error costs.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which decision minimizes expected cost in your example?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare expected costs of reviewing or accepting a fictional alert.

lessons.title: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
lessons.why: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence

concepts.name: Surprisal
concepts.explanation: Negative log probability measures how surprising an observed outcome is under a distribution.
concepts.example: Compare -log(.9) and -log(.01) for the correct class.
concepts.commonMistake: Interpreting a smaller probability as a smaller penalty.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which prediction receives the larger surprise?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare -log(.9) and -log(.01) for the correct class.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.explanation: Entropy is expected surprisal under the true distribution and measures uncertainty.
concepts.example: Compare [0.5,0.5] with [0.99,0.01] using the same logarithm base.
concepts.commonMistake: Comparing entropy values computed with different log bases without converting units.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which distribution has higher uncertainty?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare [0.5,0.5] with [0.99,0.01] using the same logarithm base.

concepts.name: Cross-entropy
concepts.explanation: Cross-entropy measures expected log loss when q models outcomes drawn from p.
concepts.example: Compute loss for a one-hot class target and predicted probabilities.
concepts.commonMistake: Passing probabilities to an API that expects unnormalized logits.
concepts.checkQuestion: What does your chosen loss function expect as input?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compute loss for a one-hot class target and predicted probabilities.

concepts.name: KL divergence
concepts.explanation: KL compares distributions directionally and is zero when they match on their support.
concepts.example: Compute both KL(p||q) and KL(q||p) for unequal binary distributions.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming KL is a symmetric distance.
concepts.checkQuestion: Why do the two directions differ?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compute both KL(p||q) and KL(q||p) for unequal binary distributions.

concepts.name: Numerical stability
concepts.explanation: Log-sum-exp computes normalization without exponentiating very large logits directly.
concepts.example: Subtract the maximum from logits [1000,1001] before exponentiation.
concepts.commonMistake: Adding arbitrary epsilon without understanding how it changes the objective.
concepts.checkQuestion: Can you obtain a finite normalized result for large logits?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Subtract the maximum from logits [1000,1001] before exponentiation.

lessons.title: Partial derivatives, Jacobians and vector gradients
lessons.why: Partial derivatives, Jacobians and vector gradients helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Partial derivatives, Jacobians and vector gradients

concepts.name: Partial derivatives
concepts.explanation: A partial derivative changes one input while holding the others fixed.
concepts.example: For f(x,y)=x*y+x*x evaluate both partial derivatives at (2,3).
concepts.commonMistake: Changing both coordinates when estimating a partial derivative.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which variable must remain fixed?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: For f(x,y)=x*y+x*x evaluate both partial derivatives at (2,3).

concepts.name: Gradient direction
concepts.explanation: The gradient points toward fastest local increase under the Euclidean norm.
concepts.example: Take a small negative-gradient step on x squared plus four y squared.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating the gradient as the parameter update without the negative sign.
concepts.checkQuestion: Does your trial step lower the loss?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Take a small negative-gradient step on x squared plus four y squared.

concepts.name: Jacobian shape
concepts.explanation: A Jacobian has one row per output and one column per input under the stated convention.
concepts.example: Write the 2 by 2 Jacobian for (x*y,x+y).
concepts.commonMistake: Dropping output dimensions when differentiating a vector-valued function.
concepts.checkQuestion: What are the axes of your Jacobian?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Write the 2 by 2 Jacobian for (x*y,x+y).

concepts.name: Chain rule composition
concepts.explanation: The derivative of composed maps combines their local derivatives in the correct order.
concepts.example: Compose a linear map with a sigmoid and compare the matrix product with autograd.
concepts.commonMistake: Multiplying derivative matrices in a dimensionally invalid order.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which intermediate shape determines the product order?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compose a linear map with a sigmoid and compare the matrix product with autograd.

concepts.name: Vector-Jacobian products
concepts.explanation: Reverse-mode differentiation propagates an output-weighted gradient without materializing the full Jacobian.
concepts.example: Differentiate a weighted sum of two outputs and compare with a manual product.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming backward always returns a full Jacobian.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which scalar objective does your backward call differentiate?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Differentiate a weighted sum of two outputs and compare with a manual product.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals, bootstrap and causal limits
lessons.why: Confidence intervals, bootstrap and causal limits helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Confidence intervals, bootstrap and causal limits

concepts.name: Sampling unit
concepts.explanation: Independent sampling units determine the meaning of uncertainty estimates.
concepts.example: Group repeated sessions by fictional user before splitting and resampling.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating many sessions from one user as independent people.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which unit should be resampled here?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Group repeated sessions by fictional user before splitting and resampling.

concepts.name: Standard error
concepts.explanation: The standard error describes variability of an estimator across samples, not variability of individual observations.
concepts.example: Compare sample standard deviation with estimated standard error of the mean.
concepts.commonMistake: Using standard deviation as the uncertainty of the mean.
concepts.checkQuestion: What changes when sample size quadruples?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare sample standard deviation with estimated standard error of the mean.

concepts.name: Bootstrap
concepts.explanation: Resampling observed units approximates the sampling distribution under assumptions about representativeness.
concepts.example: Draw 1000 seeded bootstrap samples of 80 users and form a percentile interval.
concepts.commonMistake: Bootstrapping rows when the experimental unit is a group.
concepts.checkQuestion: What assumptions can this interval not repair?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Draw 1000 seeded bootstrap samples of 80 users and form a percentile interval.

concepts.name: Confidence interpretation
concepts.explanation: A confidence procedure has long-run coverage under its assumptions; an individual fixed interval is not a probability distribution over a fixed parameter.
concepts.example: Compare coverage over 200 simulated datasets with a known mean.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming 95 percent of observations lie in a mean confidence interval.
concepts.checkQuestion: What population quantity does this interval estimate?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare coverage over 200 simulated datasets with a known mean.

concepts.name: Confounding
concepts.explanation: A shared cause can produce an association without a causal effect.
concepts.example: Generate different device mixes across groups and compare pooled and stratified means.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling an observational correlation a causal treatment effect.
concepts.checkQuestion: What randomization or additional assumptions would support a causal claim?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Generate different device mixes across groups and compare pooled and stratified means.

concepts.explanation: K-means minimises squared distance to cluster centres and is sensitive to scaling and its preferred cluster geometry.
concepts.example: Compare fitted centres for two blobs and for a curved two-moons dataset.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the k-means objective example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.

concepts.name: Initialisation and stability
concepts.explanation: Different starts can find different local solutions; inspect repeated runs and sensible n_init settings.
concepts.example: Fit several seeded runs and compare centre positions and objective values.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the initialisation and stability example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain initialisation and stability using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?

concepts.name: Density and noise
concepts.explanation: Density-based methods group connected dense regions and may label sparse points as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster.
concepts.example: Compare DBSCAN outputs under two eps values and report the number of noise points.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the density and noise example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.

concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Compare silhouette scores and visual structure on synthetic curved groups before choosing a method.

lessons.title: kNN, distance weighting and dimensionality
lessons.why: kNN, distance weighting and dimensionality helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: kNN, distance weighting and dimensionality

concepts.name: Distance metrics
concepts.explanation: Euclidean and Manhattan distance encode different notions of proximity.
concepts.example: Compare nearest neighbors before and after multiplying one feature by 100.
concepts.commonMistake: Ignoring measurement units before computing distance.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which feature dominates your unscaled distances?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare nearest neighbors before and after multiplying one feature by 100.

concepts.name: Choosing k
concepts.explanation: Small k follows local details while large k smooths decisions and can erase minority regions.
concepts.example: Plot validation error across odd k values on one fixed split.
concepts.commonMistake: Choosing k from final test performance.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which split should decide k?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Plot validation error across odd k values on one fixed split.

concepts.name: Weighted voting
concepts.explanation: Distance weighting makes nearby neighbors contribute more strongly than distant ones.
concepts.example: Handle an exact training-point match separately from inverse-distance voting.
concepts.commonMistake: Dividing by zero for identical points.
concepts.checkQuestion: What should happen when a zero-distance neighbor exists?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Handle an exact training-point match separately from inverse-distance voting.

concepts.name: Curse of dimensionality
concepts.explanation: Distances can become less discriminative as irrelevant dimensions accumulate.
concepts.example: Add 50 noise features and compare neighbor rankings and error.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming more features always improve a distance-based model.
concepts.checkQuestion: How does distance contrast change with noise dimensions?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Add 50 noise features and compare neighbor rankings and error.

concepts.name: Inference cost
concepts.explanation: Brute-force neighbor search stores training examples and compares them at inference time.
concepts.example: Measure query latency at three reference-set sizes.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating fast fitting as proof of fast prediction.
concepts.checkQuestion: What grows when the reference set doubles?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Measure query latency at three reference-set sizes.

lessons.title: PCA, explained variance and reconstruction
lessons.why: PCA, explained variance and reconstruction helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: PCA, explained variance and reconstruction

concepts.name: Centering
concepts.explanation: PCA identifies directions of variation around the training mean.
concepts.example: Subtract the training mean from both training and test rows.
concepts.commonMistake: Refitting centering on the test set.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which mean should inference reuse?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Subtract the training mean from both training and test rows.

concepts.name: Principal components
concepts.explanation: Orthogonal directions maximize successively remaining variance.
concepts.example: Rotate a correlated 2D cloud into its component coordinates.
concepts.commonMistake: Interpreting components as original input features.
concepts.checkQuestion: How is one component expressed in the original features?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Rotate a correlated 2D cloud into its component coordinates.

concepts.name: Explained variance
concepts.explanation: Variance ratios quantify retained training variation, not downstream predictive accuracy.
concepts.example: Compare two components retaining 95 percent variance with classification results.
concepts.commonMistake: Equating high retained variance with useful class information.
concepts.checkQuestion: Could a low-variance direction carry the label?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare two components retaining 95 percent variance with classification results.

concepts.name: Reconstruction
concepts.explanation: Projection followed by inverse transformation gives a low-rank approximation.
concepts.example: Plot the held-out squared reconstruction error at ranks one and two.
concepts.commonMistake: Comparing reconstruction errors under incompatible feature scaling.
concepts.checkQuestion: What baseline is needed to interpret the error?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Plot the held-out squared reconstruction error at ranks one and two.

concepts.name: Leakage and pipelines
concepts.explanation: PCA must be fitted inside the training fold during model selection.
concepts.example: Place scaling and PCA inside a cross-validation pipeline.
concepts.commonMistake: Fitting PCA on all rows before cross-validation.
concepts.checkQuestion: What information leaks from validation rows?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Place scaling and PCA inside a cross-validation pipeline.

concepts.name: Split criteria
concepts.explanation: A tree chooses a partition that reduces an impurity or regression-error objective.
concepts.example: Compute Gini impurity before and after a small binary split.
concepts.commonMistake: Selecting a split from test labels.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which rows are allowed to determine the split?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compute Gini impurity before and after a small binary split.

concepts.name: Tree depth
concepts.explanation: Deeper trees can represent finer interactions but fit noise more easily.
concepts.example: Compare training and validation errors for depths 1, 3 and unrestricted.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling perfect training accuracy sufficient validation.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which curve reveals overfitting?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare training and validation errors for depths 1, 3 and unrestricted.

concepts.name: Bagging
concepts.explanation: Bootstrap aggregation averages models fitted on resampled training sets to reduce instability.
concepts.example: Train several small trees on bootstrap samples and average predictions.
concepts.commonMistake: Confusing bootstrap training samples with a held-out test set.
concepts.checkQuestion: Why can averaging unstable estimators help?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Train several small trees on bootstrap samples and average predictions.

concepts.name: Boosting
concepts.explanation: Sequential learners correct errors under a chosen objective rather than training independently.
concepts.example: Fit a weak regression tree to residuals of an initial mean predictor.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming boosting is identical to independently averaging trees.
concepts.checkQuestion: What target does the second learner fit?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Fit a weak regression tree to residuals of an initial mean predictor.

concepts.name: Learning-rate tradeoff
concepts.explanation: Smaller boosting steps usually require more trees and still need validation.
concepts.example: Compare learning-rate and estimator-count pairs under one compute budget.
concepts.commonMistake: Increasing estimators indefinitely without monitoring validation loss.
concepts.checkQuestion: When should the boosting sequence stop?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare learning-rate and estimator-count pairs under one compute budget.

lessons.title: Model cards, licences and reproducible model selection
lessons.why: Model cards, licences and reproducible model selection helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Model cards, licences and reproducible model selection

concepts.name: Model identity
concepts.explanation: A model name alone does not identify the exact weights, tokenizer or revision used.
concepts.example: Record repository, revision and tokenizer revision in a local manifest.
concepts.commonMistake: Comparing runs from changing latest revisions as if they were identical.
concepts.checkQuestion: What must be pinned to reproduce a run?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Record repository, revision and tokenizer revision in a local manifest.

concepts.name: Model cards
concepts.explanation: A card describes intended use, training information and known limits but does not replace your own evaluation.
concepts.example: Extract supported tasks and limitations into a comparison table.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating a benchmark claim as proof of performance on your users' data.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which task-specific checks remain necessary?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Extract supported tasks and limitations into a comparison table.

concepts.name: Licence review
concepts.explanation: Weight, code and dataset licences may impose different conditions and should be recorded separately.
concepts.example: List each relevant licence link without assuming open weights means unrestricted use.
concepts.commonMistake: Equating downloadable weights with unrestricted redistribution.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which artifact's licence covers the weights?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: List each relevant licence link without assuming open weights means unrestricted use.

concepts.name: Trusted loading
concepts.explanation: Model packages can contain executable code or unsafe serialization formats.
concepts.example: Prefer supported tensor formats and inspect any request to execute remote code.
concepts.commonMistake: Enabling remote code execution simply to make loading succeed.
concepts.checkQuestion: What code is being trusted during loading?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Prefer supported tensor formats and inspect any request to execute remote code.

concepts.name: Selection evidence
concepts.explanation: Quality, latency, memory and deployment constraints jointly determine suitability.
concepts.example: Compare two models on the same 20 tasks and hardware or explicitly mark an unmeasured cell.
concepts.commonMistake: Inventing latency or quality numbers from documentation alone.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which scorecard cells are measured versus estimated?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare two models on the same 20 tasks and hardware or explicitly mark an unmeasured cell.

lessons.title: Structured output, streaming and cancellation contracts
lessons.why: Structured output, streaming and cancellation contracts helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Structured output, streaming and cancellation contracts

concepts.name: Schema enforcement
concepts.explanation: Syntactically valid JSON may still violate your application schema.
concepts.example: Reject a response with a string price where a numeric field is required.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating successful JSON parsing as full validation.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which constraints must the schema enforce?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Reject a response with a string price where a numeric field is required.

concepts.name: Partial streams
concepts.explanation: Chunks may split tokens, Unicode sequences or JSON structures before a complete response exists.
concepts.example: Split a JSON string at every position and reconstruct before validating.
concepts.commonMistake: Parsing each arbitrary chunk as a complete object.
concepts.checkQuestion: When is a response complete enough to validate?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Split a JSON string at every position and reconstruct before validating.

concepts.name: Cancellation
concepts.explanation: A user cancellation must propagate to pending work and prevent stale updates.
concepts.example: Cancel a delayed local stream and verify later chunks do not overwrite the UI.
concepts.commonMistake: Hiding the UI while leaving expensive work running.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which task and resource should cancellation close?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Cancel a delayed local stream and verify later chunks do not overwrite the UI.

concepts.name: Repair bounds
concepts.explanation: Retries or schema-repair calls must have a finite budget and preserve original evidence.
concepts.example: Allow one deterministic repair attempt, then surface a validation failure.
concepts.commonMistake: Retrying forever until a valid-looking response appears.
concepts.checkQuestion: What should the user see when repair fails?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Allow one deterministic repair attempt, then surface a validation failure.

concepts.name: Output trust
concepts.explanation: Generated strings remain untrusted when passed into HTML, SQL, shell commands or tools.
concepts.example: Render a generated script tag as text and reject a proposed shell operation.
concepts.commonMistake: Executing generated content merely because it matched a schema.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which downstream boundary still needs validation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Render a generated script tag as text and reject a proposed shell operation.

concepts.name: Preference pairs
concepts.explanation: A chosen and rejected response encode a relative judgment for a specific prompt and rubric.
concepts.example: Write two responses differing in factual support while keeping style comparable.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming longer responses are automatically preferred.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which criterion explains the preference label?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Write two responses differing in factual support while keeping style comparable.

concepts.name: Label quality
concepts.explanation: Ambiguous or inconsistent pairs can teach undesired shortcuts.
concepts.example: Blind-review five conflicting pairs and record disagreements.
concepts.commonMistake: Forcing a label when reviewers disagree without a rubric.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which pairs should be revised or excluded?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Blind-review five conflicting pairs and record disagreements.

concepts.name: Reference policy
concepts.explanation: Preference objectives may compare a trained policy with a reference to constrain changes.
concepts.example: Compare chosen/rejected log-probability ratios for two toy policies.
concepts.commonMistake: Ignoring the reference term when interpreting a DPO-style objective.
concepts.checkQuestion: What behavior does the reference constrain?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare chosen/rejected log-probability ratios for two toy policies.

concepts.name: Overoptimization
concepts.explanation: Improvement on a preference proxy can worsen real task performance.
concepts.example: Construct a pairwise judge that rewards verbosity and inspect its failure cases.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating preference-win rate as complete evidence of quality.
concepts.checkQuestion: What independent checks catch reward shortcuts?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Construct a pairwise judge that rewards verbosity and inspect its failure cases.

concepts.checkQuestion: Which cases were withheld from optimization?

concepts.name: Modality preprocessing
concepts.explanation: Images, audio and text need different preprocessing contracts before a model consumes them.

concepts.checkQuestion: Which preprocessing choices affect interpretation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Record image dimensions, color channels and normalization alongside a caption.

concepts.name: Alignment
concepts.explanation: Cross-modal inputs must refer to the same example and compatible time or spatial units.
concepts.example: Pair a generated image with a caption using a stable example ID.
concepts.commonMistake: Joining audio and captions by list position after filtering one list.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which key prevents misaligned pairs?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Pair a generated image with a caption using a stable example ID.

concepts.name: Budget accounting
concepts.explanation: Image patches and audio duration can consume context or compute differently from text.
concepts.example: Set explicit image dimensions and duration limits in a request validator.
concepts.commonMistake: Applying a text-character limit as the only multimodal resource bound.
concepts.checkQuestion: What limit controls each modality?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Set explicit image dimensions and duration limits in a request validator.

concepts.name: Grounding limits
concepts.explanation: A generated description may claim details not visible in the input.
concepts.example: Flag a fixture caption claiming a hidden object that the image does not contain.
concepts.commonMistake: Treating fluent visual descriptions as evidence of visibility.
concepts.checkQuestion: What source supports each claimed observation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Flag a fixture caption claiming a hidden object that the image does not contain.

concepts.name: Evaluation slices

concepts.checkQuestion: Which failure slice matters for your user task?

concepts.example: Search a fixed subset and compare top-five results with exhaustive scoring.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming faster search preserves all relevant neighbors.
concepts.checkQuestion: How much recall is lost at this candidate budget?

concepts.name: Index parameters
concepts.explanation: Construction and query parameters trade memory, build time and query recall.

concepts.checkQuestion: Which variables must remain fixed?

concepts.name: Supply-chain provenance
concepts.explanation: Downloaded models, plugins and dependencies are separate trust decisions from a model's textual answers.
concepts.example: Record origin and revision for every executable dependency in a toy manifest.
concepts.commonMistake: Trusting an artifact solely because its name resembles a popular package.
concepts.checkQuestion: How do you verify the exact artifact identity?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Record origin and revision for every executable dependency in a toy manifest.

concepts.name: Unsafe output handling
concepts.explanation: Generated text must not become executable HTML, SQL or shell syntax without a trusted boundary.
concepts.example: Test a response containing an HTML handler and a proposed SQL write.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming a system prompt prevents downstream injection.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which operation enforces the boundary outside the model?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Test a response containing an HTML handler and a proposed SQL write.

concepts.name: Retrieval poisoning

lessons.title: Backup, restore and data recovery drills
lessons.why: Backup, restore and data recovery drills helps you make explainable engineering decisions and test failure cases. Build the experiment below before relying on the concept in an AI system.
lessons.summary: Backup, restore and data recovery drills

concepts.name: Recovery point objective
concepts.explanation: RPO describes the tolerated loss window, not the time needed to restart a process.
concepts.example: Compare hourly and daily backups against a two-hour loss tolerance.
concepts.commonMistake: Confusing recovery point with recovery time.
concepts.checkQuestion: How much data could the schedule lose?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Compare hourly and daily backups against a two-hour loss tolerance.

concepts.name: Recovery time objective
concepts.explanation: RTO bounds acceptable restoration duration including validation.
concepts.example: Time a restore into a clean local database and run a query smoke test.
concepts.commonMistake: Timing only file copying and excluding verification.
concepts.checkQuestion: When is recovery actually complete?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Time a restore into a clean local database and run a query smoke test.

concepts.name: Consistent backups
concepts.explanation: A backup must represent a recoverable database state rather than an arbitrary copy during writes.
concepts.example: Use the database backup mechanism and compare with a naive live file copy.
concepts.commonMistake: Assuming every copied data directory is transactionally consistent.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which method guarantees a consistent snapshot?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Use the database backup mechanism and compare with a naive live file copy.

concepts.name: Restore verification
concepts.explanation: A backup is useful only if it can be restored and checked.
concepts.example: Verify expected rows, constraints and application queries after restoration.
concepts.commonMistake: Calling an uploaded archive a tested backup.
concepts.checkQuestion: Which checks prove restored data is usable?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Verify expected rows, constraints and application queries after restoration.

concepts.name: Retention and access
concepts.explanation: Backup retention and permissions should match data sensitivity and recovery needs.
concepts.example: Keep two disposable generations and restrict access to the test backup folder.
concepts.commonMistake: Making backups readable to everyone because they are offline.
concepts.checkQuestion: Who can read or delete the recovery artifacts?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce this example and test one changed input: Keep two disposable generations and restrict access to the test backup folder.

lessons.title: Phase 1 · Distributed processing with Spark
lessons.why: Move from single-machine transformations to distributed processing, and learn to explain Spark plans, shuffles, skew and performance rather than treating Spark as a black box.
lessons.summary: Move from single-machine transformations to distributed processing, and learn to explain Spark plans, shuffles, skew and performance rather than treating Spark as a black box.

concepts.name: Spark architecture and execution
concepts.explanation: The driver builds a plan, executors run tasks, and a cluster manager allocates resources; jobs contain stages, which contain tasks mapped from a DAG. Lazy transformations are evaluated by actions. Catalyst optimizes plans and Tungsten improves execution; use explain() to inspect logical and physical plans.
concepts.example: Trace a filter, join and aggregation from a DataFrame action to its jobs, stages and tasks in the Spark UI.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the spark architecture and execution example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain spark architecture and execution using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Trace a filter, join and aggregation from a DataFrame action to its jobs, stages and tasks in the Spark UI.

concepts.name: Core APIs
concepts.explanation: RDDs explain Spark's distributed collection model; DataFrames provide schema-aware select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, agg and orderBy; Spark SQL runs through temporary views. Know that typed Datasets are mainly a Scala/Java API concern in a PySpark workflow.
concepts.example: Create a DataFrame, register it as a temporary view, run the same aggregation in SQL and DataFrame syntax, and compare the results.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the core apis example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain core apis using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?

concepts.name: Partitions, shuffles and skew
concepts.explanation: Partitions distribute work and default counts depend on input and configuration. repartition() redistributes data; coalesce() can reduce partitions with less movement. Grouping, joins, distinct, ordering and repartitioning can trigger shuffles, with map/reduce stages and disk spill. Detect skew through task-duration spread; mitigate with salting, broadcast joins or a suitable partition strategy.
concepts.example: Use a deliberately skewed key, inspect task durations, then compare a salted aggregation with the unsalted result.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the partitions, shuffles and skew example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain partitions, shuffles and skew using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Use a deliberately skewed key, inspect task durations, then compare a salted aggregation with the unsalted result.

concepts.name: Join planning
concepts.explanation: Broadcast hash joins, shuffle sort-merge joins and shuffle hash joins trade memory for network and sorting work. Spark can broadcast below its size threshold or use a broadcast hint; join reordering and predicate pushdown can reduce work. Skewed keys may need their own strategy.
concepts.example: Compare explain() plans for a small-dimension broadcast join and a large-large join, then push a selective filter before the join.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the join planning example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain join planning using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Compare explain() plans for a small-dimension broadcast join and a large-large join, then push a selective filter before the join.

concepts.name: Memory, caching and spill
concepts.explanation: MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK and DISK_ONLY have different recomputation and storage costs; serialized and deserialized storage trade CPU for memory. cache() uses a default persistence level; persist() selects one explicitly. Understand executor execution/storage memory and unpersist materialized data when it is no longer needed.
concepts.example: Persist a reused DataFrame, inspect storage in the Spark UI, and unpersist it after the last dependent action.
concepts.commonMistake: Reusing stale state without checking its identity, scope and version.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain memory, caching and spill using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Persist a reused DataFrame, inspect storage in the Spark UI, and unpersist it after the last dependent action.

concepts.name: Performance diagnosis
concepts.explanation: Use Jobs, Stages, Storage and Executors in the Spark UI to find long stages, skewed tasks, excess shuffles and GC pressure. Adaptive Query Execution can coalesce partitions and handle some skew. Parquet column pruning and predicate pushdown reduce I/O when queries select few columns or rows.
concepts.example: Capture a baseline and an optimized run, explain the changed plan and report task-time and input-size differences.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the performance diagnosis example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.
concepts.checkQuestion: Explain performance diagnosis using the example. What result do you expect, and what changed input would invalidate that expectation?
concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Capture a baseline and an optimized run, explain the changed plan and report task-time and input-size differences.

concepts.name: UDFs
concepts.explanation: Python UDFs pay row-by-row serialization and Py4J costs; Pandas UDFs use Arrow-backed vectorization and can help for operations unavailable in Spark's built-ins. Built-in Spark SQL functions are generally preferable because Spark can optimize them.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.explanation: Window.partitionBy() and orderBy() define per-group ordered calculations. row_number, rank and dense_rank differ on ties; lag and lead access neighboring rows, while window frames support running totals and moving averages.

concepts.name: Structured Streaming introduction
concepts.explanation: A streaming DataFrame shares the batch DataFrame API but executes incrementally, commonly in micro-batches. Watermarks bound state while allowing late events; append, update and complete output modes have different result semantics.

concepts.name: Deployment and I/O
concepts.explanation: Local, standalone and cluster execution differ in resource placement; client and cluster deploy modes place the driver differently. spark-submit exposes the main job configuration. Read and write Parquet, CSV, JDBC and cloud-storage paths with explicit schemas and safe credentials.

lessons.title: Phase 2 · Orchestration mastery with Airflow
lessons.why: Go beyond introductory DAGs to design, test, operate and debug reliable workflows that coordinate data systems without hiding business logic in orchestration code.
lessons.summary: Go beyond introductory DAGs to design, test, operate and debug reliable workflows that coordinate data systems without hiding business logic in orchestration code.

concepts.name: Airflow architecture
concepts.explanation: The Scheduler parses DAG files and decides what is ready; the Webserver presents the UI; an Executor dispatches work; the Metadata DB stores state; and the Triggerer handles deferrable work. Sequential, Local, Celery and Kubernetes executors trade simplicity for parallel and distributed capacity. Know where DAG files are discovered and how parsing works.
concepts.example: Trace one scheduled task from DAG parsing through scheduler state, executor dispatch and metadata updates.
concepts.commonMistake: Claiming the airflow architecture example is correct without checking its inputs, output and failure case.

concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Trace one scheduled task from DAG parsing through scheduler state, executor dispatch and metadata updates.

concepts.name: DAG configuration
concepts.explanation: DAG schedule, start_date, catchup and max_active_runs determine when runs are created and how much work may overlap. Task dependencies can use >>, <<, set_upstream and set_downstream; pools, priority_weight and task concurrency limit contention.
concepts.example: Configure a daily DAG with a historical start date, disable catchup, cap active runs and show which logical dates are scheduled.

concepts.name: TaskFlow, XCom and branching
concepts.explanation: TaskFlow uses @dag and @task and is the preferred style for new Python DAGs; classic operators remain useful. XCom passes small metadata, not large datasets. BranchPythonOperator or @task.branch chooses paths, while trigger rules such as all_success, all_failed, one_success and none_failed control downstream execution.

concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Build a TaskFlow DAG that branches on a data-quality result, passes only a partition identifier by XCom and joins paths with an explicit trigger rule.

concepts.name: Dynamic task mapping
concepts.explanation: expand() and partial() create mapped tasks at run time from a collection; a static loop creates tasks during DAG definition. Map over a bounded list of tables, files or partitions, and understand limits on mapped task counts.
concepts.example: Map a validation task over a run-time list of table names and contrast it with a small static DAG.

concepts.exercise: Reproduce and explain this worked case, then test an edge case: Map a validation task over a run-time list of table names and contrast it with a small static DAG.

concepts.name: Custom components
concepts.explanation: Custom Operators subclass BaseOperator; Hooks wrap external connections; Sensors wait using poke or reschedule mode with a poke interval and timeout. Prefer maintained provider components when they satisfy the use case; avoid building custom abstractions without a concrete need.

concepts.name: Reliability and production
concepts.explanation: Retries, retry_delay and exponential backoff recover transient failures; timeouts bound work. SLA settings and callbacks communicate missed expectations. Tasks should be idempotent so retries and backfills do not duplicate or corrupt data. Catchup and CLI backfills need safe ranges; success/failure callbacks can notify Slack or email.

lessons.title: Phase 3 · Streaming and CDC with Kafka
lessons.why: Ingest changes as durable ordered events, understand delivery guarantees and schemas, and operate a CDC path from a transactional database into a lake or warehouse.
lessons.summary: Ingest changes as durable ordered events, understand delivery guarantees and schemas, and operate a CDC path from a transactional database into a lake or warehouse.

concepts.name: Kafka foundations
concepts.explanation: Topics contain partitions; offsets identify records and ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across a topic. Brokers form clusters and replicate partitions with a replication factor and in-sync replicas. Producers choose partitioning and acknowledgements (acks=0/1/all); consumer groups distribute partitions and rebalance. Retention can delete by time/size or compact by key.
concepts.example: Produce keyed customer events and show that matching keys retain partition order while unrelated partitions have no global ordering.

concepts.name: Delivery semantics
concepts.explanation: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once depend on when offsets are committed and what is transactional. Idempotent producers reduce duplicate writes; consumers choose automatic or manual commits. Kafka transactions coordinate records and offsets but do not make arbitrary external side effects exactly once.

concepts.name: Schema management
concepts.explanation: A schema registry governs independently deployed producer and consumer contracts. Backward, forward and full compatibility define which old/new readers and writers interoperate. Avro, Protobuf and JSON Schema trade compactness, tooling and flexibility; schema evolution must be planned before breaking downstream readers.

Initial snapshots and incremental capture have different behavior; handle deletes, source schema changes and out-of-order events explicitly.

lessons.title: Phase 4 · Lakehouse formats and storage internals
lessons.why: Understand what happens beneath analytical tables, and how transactional table formats, catalogs and query engines make object storage usable for evolving batch and streaming workloads.
lessons.summary: Understand what happens beneath analytical tables, and how transactional table formats, catalogs and query engines make object storage usable for evolving batch and streaming workloads.

concepts.name: File formats
concepts.explanation: Row-oriented formats suit record-at-a-time access; columnar formats suit analytical scans. Parquet stores row groups, column chunks, pages and footer metadata; column statistics enable pruning and predicate pushdown. Snappy, Gzip and Zstd trade compression ratio for CPU; dictionary and run-length encoding exploit repeated values. ORC is another analytical format and Avro is common for CDC events.

concepts.name: Why table formats matter
concepts.explanation: Raw Parquet on a filesystem becomes difficult as tables grow: small files increase metadata and planning overhead, while concurrent writers can conflict without transaction coordination.

concepts.name: Iceberg and Delta internals
concepts.explanation: Iceberg and Delta add metadata and transaction layers over object storage. Iceberg manifests, manifest lists and snapshots describe files; both formats use optimistic concurrency for ACID-like updates. Time travel queries a prior snapshot; schema evolution avoids rewriting all data. Iceberg supports partition evolution and hidden partitioning.

concepts.name: Table maintenance
concepts.explanation: Compaction merges small files; snapshot expiration or vacuuming removes eligible historical data. Sorting or Z-ordering improves data skipping for selected query patterns; Iceberg sort orders and manifest rewrites keep metadata useful. Retention must be balanced with recovery and compliance needs.

concepts.name: Catalogs
concepts.explanation: A catalog resolves table names to metadata locations. Hive Metastore is a traditional option; AWS Glue is managed; Nessie provides Git-like versioning for Iceberg; REST catalogs expose a service interface used by a growing ecosystem.

Engines use table metadata to skip files and partitions; Spark suits heavy ETL while Trino suits interactive/federated SQL workloads.

concepts.name: dbt project and DAG
concepts.explanation: A dbt project organizes models, sources, seeds, snapshots, macros, tests, exposures and analyses. view, table, incremental and ephemeral materializations trade freshness, compute and reuse. ref() and source() create dependency edges; dbt build runs the selected resource graph with tests, while dbt run and dbt test focus on transformations and checks.

concepts.name: Monitoring and alerting
concepts.explanation: Freshness catches stale tables; volume catches row-count drops/spikes; schema drift catches changed columns or types; distribution monitoring can surface anomalies. Route alerts with owner, impact and runbook context to avoid alert fatigue.

concepts.name: Lightweight anomaly detection
concepts.explanation: Rolling averages and standard-deviation thresholds can detect simple changes. Rule-based, statistical and ML-based methods differ in complexity and explainability; use simple rules when sufficient.

concepts.explanation: Place checks after ingestion, after transformation or both depending on the failure and recovery boundary. Fail fast for invalid data that must not propagate; quarantine recoverable bad records. Connect Airflow check failures to real alert callbacks and track quality measures over time.

concepts.name: Docker in depth
concepts.explanation: Multi-stage builds reduce production image size; layer caching speeds repeated builds. Volumes persist container data, while bind mounts connect host paths. Bridge networking enables container communication; Compose healthchecks, depends_on conditions and resource limits shape local stacks.

concepts.name: Kubernetes basics
concepts.explanation: Pods run containers; Deployments manage replicas; Services provide stable access; ConfigMaps and Secrets supply configuration. Jobs and CronJobs run finite or scheduled work; Namespaces isolate projects. Resource requests and limits affect placement and throttling. Practice kubectl get, describe, logs and exec with minikube or kind.

lessons.title: Phase 1 · ML engineering and MLOps
lessons.why: Connect reliable data engineering to reproducible model training and serving, while making feature correctness, model lifecycle and production feedback explicit.
lessons.summary: Connect reliable data engineering to reproducible model training and serving, while making feature correctness, model lifecycle and production feedback explicit.

concepts.name: Feature engineering pipelines
concepts.explanation: Feature pipelines are data pipelines with an ML consumer. Batch and online/real-time feature computation differ in latency and freshness. Feature stores support reuse but must address training-serving skew and point-in-time correctness. Feast models entities and feature views over offline and online stores; point-in-time joins prevent future information leaking into training.

concepts.name: Model training pipelines
concepts.explanation: Structure training as extraction, features, train, evaluate and register steps. Reproducibility pins data, code and hyperparameters together. Grid/random search provide baselines; Bayesian optimization may be worth the extra complexity for expensive searches. Cross-validation should be represented in the pipeline, not hidden in an ad hoc notebook.

concepts.name: Experiment tracking and registry
concepts.explanation: MLflow Tracking stores parameters, metrics and artifacts; its Model Registry supports lifecycle states such as staging, production and archived. Record metrics, hyperparameters, data version/hash and environment so a run can be compared and reproduced.

concepts.name: Deployment patterns
concepts.explanation: Batch inference processes a scheduled dataset; online inference serves requests with tighter latency needs. Serve through FastAPI and a container when appropriate. Shadow and canary deployments compare or gradually expose a model before full rollout.

concepts.name: Monitoring and drift
concepts.explanation: Data drift changes input distributions; concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and outcomes. Monitor prediction distributions as well as uptime and latency. Retraining may be scheduled or triggered by drift, but requires a verified policy. Capture ground truth to evaluate real-world performance and avoid unsafe feedback loops.

concepts.name: Deep learning foundations
concepts.explanation: Perceptrons, activation functions, backpropagation and gradient descent provide conceptual fluency without derivation-heavy mathematics. CNNs and RNNs address image and sequence tasks; transformers largely replaced RNNs for many sequence workloads. Batch size, learning rate, Adam/SGD, dropout and weight decay shape training.

concepts.name: Transformer architecture
concepts.explanation: Self-attention is the core interaction mechanism. Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder designs correspond broadly to BERT-, GPT- and T5-style tasks. Positional encoding and multi-head attention help represent order and multiple relation patterns; this vocabulary helps interpret model cards.

concepts.explanation: Pretraining, fine-tuning and instruction tuning change different parts of model behavior. LoRA/QLoRA adapt fewer parameters than full fine-tuning; prompting may be preferable when data, cost or maintenance do not justify training. Few-shot and structured-output prompts are practical tools. In-context learning uses examples in the prompt without changing model weights.

concepts.explanation: Benchmark suites, LLM-as-judge and human evaluation measure different properties; plausible prose is not evaluation. Hallucination can be mitigated with grounded retrieval and calibrated uncertainty signals, but not eliminated by a single prompt. Discuss bias and safety at a practical level and set clear product limits.

concepts.name: LLM and RAG stack
concepts.explanation: Embeddings map text to vectors; cosine similarity and dot product rank candidates. pgvector, Qdrant and Weaviate are vector-storage options. Fixed-size, semantic and overlapping chunks have different context trade-offs. Dense, hybrid dense+BM25 and reranked retrieval are alternatives. A RAG pipeline ingests, chunks, embeds, stores, retrieves and generates; evaluate recall@k separately from answer quality.

concepts.explanation: Tools use function calling to invoke bounded actions. A single agent with tools differs from multi-agent handoff in complexity and coordination. Identify practical DE/AI uses before adopting agents; LangChain/LangGraph are options, as is a lean custom workflow.

concepts.name: System design framework
concepts.explanation: Clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, deep-dive into the critical path and explain trade-offs.
